prompt: What does BigQuery ask you to size before you can run a query?
hint: Compare it with the Cloud SQL instance of lesson 6.

choices.text: A number of nodes and a node type
choices.why: That is a cluster, and BigQuery has none: no instance, no node type.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. Storage grows as rows are written and compute is given slots per query.

choices.text: The disk of the dataset, in GiB
choices.why: There is no disk to provision; you are billed for what the tables hold.

choices.text: How many slots each query will use
choices.why: On demand, BigQuery decides that per query, up to 2,000 shared by the project.

prompt: An analyst in the project `quitanda-analytics` queries `planner-dev.quitanda.orders`. Which project pays for the query?
hint: A query is a job, and a job belongs to somebody.

choices.text: `planner-dev`, because it owns the table
choices.why: The owner pays to store it; the pricing page says the owner is not charged when the data is read.

choices.text: Both, half each
choices.why: There is no split: one job, one project billed.

choices.text: The analyst's own
choices.why: Right. Compute goes to the reader's project and storage to the owner's.

choices.text: Neither, as long as both are in one organisation
choices.why: Sharing an organisation does not make a query free.

prompt: What happens between two stages of a BigQuery query, such as a read stage and a sum per store?
hint: The second stage needs every row of one store in one place.

choices.text: They are shuffled to the next stage's slots, by key
choices.why: Right. That is the shuffle, and lesson 16 reads it in the execution graph.

choices.text: The table is copied to a larger machine
choices.why: Nothing is copied to a machine; slots read storage over the network.

choices.text: Each slot writes a temporary table the next one loads
choices.why: There is no load between stages; the rows go through a memory tier.

choices.text: Nothing: one slot runs the whole query
choices.why: A stage that reads a large table is split among many slots at once.

prompt: Which of these are decisions a BigQuery user makes that change the bill? Choose all that apply.
hint: BigQuery leaves out several things a cluster warehouse asks for.

choices.text: How a table is partitioned
choices.why: Yes. Lesson 15.

choices.text: How a table is clustered
choices.why: Yes. Lesson 15 too.

choices.text: Which column distributes the rows across nodes
choices.why: No table lives on a particular machine, so there is no distribution key.

choices.text: When to vacuum a table
choices.why: The storage is Google's to arrange; there is no vacuum to schedule.

choices.text: Which columns a query names
choices.why: Yes. Compute reads only those columns, and on demand you pay for what it reads.

prompt: Why does this course run BigQuery's SQL in DuckDB rather than in an emulator?
hint: Think of what Google publishes, and what this lesson is about.

choices.text: DuckDB is BigQuery's open-source engine
choices.why: They are unrelated projects; DuckDB's SQL follows PostgreSQL.

choices.text: The BigQuery emulator needs a paid account
choices.why: There is no BigQuery emulator from Google, paid or free.

choices.text: Google publishes no BigQuery emulator
choices.why: Right. A lab with the right rows and the wrong bill would teach the wrong half.

choices.text: `bq` was too old to talk to an emulator
choices.why: `bq` refused for want of an account; there is nothing for it to talk to.

prompt: Which of these does DuckDB measure for real in these lessons? Choose all that apply.
hint: DuckDB is free, runs on your cores, and writes no Capacitor.

choices.text: The rows a query returns
choices.why: Yes. The SQL runs for real on the same files.

choices.text: Which folders a filter on `dt` skips
choices.why: Yes. It reads the date out of `dt=` folder names and prunes them.

choices.text: The dollars BigQuery would bill
choices.why: DuckDB costs nothing; the bill is computed from Google's documentation.

choices.text: The slot-hours a query would use
choices.why: DuckDB runs on your laptop's cores; its time says nothing about slots.

choices.text: A table's physical bytes in BigQuery
choices.why: Those are Capacitor's; Parquet's size is only a clue.

prompt: A query takes 0.3 seconds in DuckDB on Quitanda's orders. What does that tell you about the same query in BigQuery?
hint: One runs on a laptop and the other on slots it is given.

choices.text: It will use about 0.3 slot-seconds
choices.why: Slot time depends on how many slots BigQuery gives it, which DuckDB cannot know.

choices.text: Nothing about its slots or its bill
choices.why: Right. The rows match; the cost is computed apart.

choices.text: It will cost less than a cent
choices.why: On demand the bill follows bytes read, not time, and has a minimum.

choices.text: It will be slower in BigQuery
choices.why: Nothing measured here can say that either way.

prompt: Why is `make_orders.py` seeded with `random.Random(13)`?
hint: Think of the numbers in the transcripts.

choices.text: So that BigQuery accepts the files
choices.why: BigQuery does not care how the values were chosen.

choices.text: So every run writes the same orders
choices.why: Right. The time differs; the rows do not.

choices.text: To make the program run faster
choices.why: A seed fixes the choices; it does not speed them up.

choices.text: To give each day the same number of orders
choices.why: `WEEKDAY` and the random factor still vary the days; the seed only repeats them.

prompt: After `bq load` of the Parquet files from `gs://quitanda-curated-prod/orders/` into a table, what happens to the objects in the bucket?
hint: The load copies; does anything tidy up?

choices.text: They are moved into BigQuery and the bucket is emptied
choices.why: A load reads the files; it does not remove them.

choices.text: They become long-term storage after the load
choices.why: Long-term is a BigQuery rate for tables; it does not apply to Cloud Storage objects.

choices.text: They stay, billed as objects as well as a table
choices.why: Right. Nothing deletes them for you.

choices.text: They are deleted after seven days of time travel
choices.why: Time travel is about a table's past versions, not the source files.

prompt: A folder named `dt=2026-08-01` follows the convention called ___ partitioning, which both DuckDB and BigQuery read a column out of.
hint: The name of an Apache project.

prompt: How many logical bytes does BigQuery count for the `STRING` value `'Butantã'`?
hint: Two bytes, plus its length in UTF-8, not in characters.

choices.why: That is its length in characters, without the 2 bytes of overhead.
That is 2 + 7: it counts `ã` as one byte, and in UTF-8 it is two.
Right. 8 UTF-8 bytes plus 2.
That is its UTF-8 length, without the 2 bytes BigQuery adds.

prompt: A table has 2,000,000 rows and three columns: an `INT64`, a `DATE` and a `BOOL`, none of them null. What is its logical size, in bytes?
hint: 8 + 8 + 1 bytes a row.

prompt: Half the values in a `STRING` column are `NULL`. What do those values add to the column's logical size?
hint: The documentation has a row for `NULL`.

choices.text: 2 bytes each, the overhead of a string
choices.why: The 2 bytes belong to a value; a `NULL` has none.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. A `NULL` of any type counts 0 bytes.

choices.text: The average length of the other half
choices.why: Nothing is imputed; a `NULL` is counted as 0.

choices.text: 8 bytes each, like a fixed-width value
choices.why: Even an `INT64` that is `NULL` counts 0 bytes.

prompt: Quitanda's 99,177,572 logical bytes sit in 32,451,790 bytes of Parquet. What does that ratio of 3.06 tell you about BigQuery's physical bytes for the same table?
hint: Parquet and Capacitor are two formats.

choices.text: They are 32,451,790 bytes, since both formats are columnar
choices.why: Both are columnar and compressed, and they are still different formats.

choices.text: Physical bytes equal logical bytes until the table goes long-term
choices.why: Long-term changes the rate, not the size.

choices.text: They will be exactly a third of the logical bytes
choices.why: Nothing here measures BigQuery's compression, so no exact figure follows.

choices.text: Only that these columns compress well; the number itself is in `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLE_STORAGE`
choices.why: Right. The Parquet ratio is a clue, and the real one is reported per table.

prompt: A partition of `orders` has not been written to for 91 days, and analysts query it every morning. Which rate does it pay?
hint: Check the page's list of what resets the clock.

choices.text: Long-term
choices.why: Right. Querying does not reset the 90 days.

choices.text: Active, because it is read daily
choices.why: Reads do not count as modifications.

choices.text: Active for the hours it is being read
choices.why: The rate follows writes, never reads.

choices.text: Neither: a queried partition is billed as compute
choices.why: The query is billed as compute; the partition is still stored and billed as storage.

prompt: Under logical billing in southamerica-east1, what does 2,048 GiB cost in a month if it is all long-term? Give USD to two decimal places.
hint: 0.016 USD per GiB-month.

prompt: Under the active rates, physical billing is cheaper than logical only when the data compresses by more than what?
hint: Divide one rate by the other.

choices.text: 2.19 to one
choices.why: That is the long-term crossing, 0.035 ÷ 0.016.

choices.text: 3.04 to one
Any compression at all, since physical bytes are fewer
choices.why: Fewer bytes at three times the rate: the ratio has to beat the rate's.

choices.text: 2 to one
choices.why: At 2 to one, 0.07 ÷ 2 is still above 0.023.

prompt: Quitanda rewrites the last 30 days of a large table every night to correct late orders. Which storage billing model does that habit push against?
hint: Where do the replaced bytes go, and who pays for them?

choices.text: Physical: the replaced bytes are billed as time travel and fail-safe
choices.why: Right. Under logical billing the same history costs nothing.

choices.text: Logical, because rewritten data is counted twice
choices.why: Logical billing has no charge for time travel or fail-safe.

choices.text: Neither: rewrites only affect the query bill
choices.why: They also reset the 90-day clock and keep old bytes for time travel.

choices.text: Long-term, which a rewrite turns off for the whole table and every partition in it, every night
choices.why: Long-term is a rate, not a model; and on a partitioned table only the rewritten partitions go active.

prompt: Match each of BigQuery's meters to what it counts.
hint: One of the right-hand options is not billed at all.

pairs.right: The uncompressed bytes of each value, by type, per GiB-month
The compressed bytes stored, time travel and fail-safe included
The logical bytes of the columns a query reads, per TiB

right_distractors: A batch load from Cloud Storage

prompt: Quitanda's whole orders table is 0.092 GiB and it is queried hundreds of times a day. Where is its cost?
hint: Compare it with the free storage each month.

choices.text: In storage, because it is queried so often
choices.why: Storage does not depend on how often a table is read.

choices.text: In the queries: its storage fits inside the free 10 GiB
choices.why: Right. Storing these orders is free; reading them is the bill.

choices.text: In time travel, since it is partitioned by day
choices.why: Partitioning has nothing to do with time travel charges, which only physical billing has.

choices.text: Nowhere: tables under 1 TiB are free to query
choices.why: The free TiB is per month of queries, not per table.

prompt: Which of these numbers in this lesson were measured, rather than taken from Google's documentation or computed from it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two things ran: DuckDB, and fake-gcs-server.

choices.text: The table has 1,245,118 rows
choices.why: Yes. DuckDB counted them.

choices.text: The Parquet files are 32,451,790 bytes
choices.why: Yes. `du` and the emulator both printed it.

choices.text: A `STRING` costs 2 bytes plus its UTF-8 length
choices.why: That is the documented rule; DuckDB only applied it.

choices.text: Physical billing would cost 13.14 USD a month for 1 TiB, nine tenths long-term
choices.why: Computed from the page's rates, at a ratio nobody measured.

choices.text: Time travel lasts seven days by default
choices.why: From Google's documentation; nothing here keeps a past version.
